proviso

pruh-VY-zoh -- from the Latin legal phrase proviso quod ('it being provided that'), from providere ('to foresee, provide'). · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Proviso is a condition or stipulation attached to an agreement.

The estate's will included a proviso denying the inheritance to any heir who contested it in court.

Example

The publishing contract included a proviso letting the author reclaim all rights if the book ever went out of print for more than two years.

That specific, spelled-out condition attached to an otherwise finished agreement -- the fine print that could change everything -- is exactly what a proviso is.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

clause: A clause is any distinct section of a legal document, whether it grants a right, sets a date, or demands nothing at all. A proviso is a particular kind of content: one condition the agreement hangs on. Every proviso is stated in a clause, but most clauses carry no condition.

term: A term is any one of the points an agreement settles -- the price, the dates, who does what. A proviso is narrower and sharper: one specific condition attached to the deal, the 'only if' that can undo everything. Most terms simply state facts; a proviso sets a test.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

guarantee: a firm, unconditional promise

certainty: something that is completely sure, with no conditions attached

Where it sits · how firmly the condition is demanded

understanding → proviso → stipulation

understanding vs. proviso: An understanding is gentler than a proviso: it is an informal, often unwritten expectation between the people involved, while a proviso is a definite condition spelled out inside the agreement itself.

stipulation vs. proviso: Stipulation is stronger than proviso: a proviso quietly attaches a condition to an agreement, while a stipulation is a firm, explicit demand -- volunteer ten hours a month, or lose the scholarship.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — vid-/vis-: to see (Latin (videre))

Put it together: Proviso comes from the Latin legal phrase proviso quod, 'it being provided that,' built on providere ('to see ahead, provide for') -- a proviso is a condition someone saw ahead of time and wrote in to protect against.

Use the root in a new word: evident: It was evident from the very first page that the report had been rushed.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Proviso is a formal word most at home in contracts, treaties, and agreements -- it points to one specific condition rather than an agreement's terms in general.
